summary: Give a group of servers one address, then decide which server handles each request.
goals: Why a group of servers needs one front door
How health checks route around a failed server
How to avoid a single point of failure in the load balancer
How layer 7 routing and gradual deploys work

steps.callout: Adding servers helps only when requests are spread across them.
The servers behind a load balancer are its pool (also called a target group).

body: How does the load balancer (LB) choose a server? The simplest rule is round robin: A, then B, then C, then A again. It is simple and shares requests evenly when servers have similar power and requests take about the same amount of work.
steps.callout: Weighted round robin sends a larger share to stronger servers. For example, A : B : C = 2 : 1 : 1.
Round robin counts requests. It does not know how much work each request takes.
Other choices include least response time, IP hash (send the same client to the same server), and power of two choices (sample two servers and pick the less busy one).
A single point of failure (SPOF) is one component whose failure can stop the service. Health checks help avoid a single failed server becoming one.

body: We removed one single point of failure and created another. Every request now passes through one load balancer. If it fails, users cannot reach the healthy servers behind it.
steps.callout: Any component every request depends on needs a backup.
Cloud load balancers, such as AWS ELB and Google Cloud Load Balancing, run across multiple machines and zones for you.

body: The active load balancer fails. The standby notices that heartbeats stopped, takes over the virtual IP, and starts forwarding traffic. Clients keep using the same address. A few requests already in progress may need to be retried.
steps.callout: This is active–passive failover: a standby takes over when the active component fails. The same pattern can protect databases, caches, and queues.

body: There are two kinds of load balancer. A layer 4 balancer sees IP addresses and ports, then forwards connections. A layer 7 balancer can read the HTTP request. It can route by URL path: /api/* to API servers and /images/* to an image service. Each group can be scaled and deployed separately.
steps.callout: Layer 7 balancers can also route by host name, header, or cookie. They can handle TLS encryption, caching, or compression.

body: Time to release version 2. A rolling deploy updates one server at a time. First, the load balancer drains that server: it sends no new requests there, but lets requests already running finish. The server is updated, checked for health, and added back. Here C has version 2, B is draining, and A is waiting. Users should not see an error.
steps.callout: With a blue-green deploy, bring up a complete version 2 pool, switch traffic to it, and switch back if something goes wrong.

body:
• A load balancer gives a server pool one stable address.
  • Round robin is simple; least connections adapts when requests take different amounts of time.
  • Health checks remove failed servers from the pool.
  • The load balancer also needs redundancy: use active–passive failover with a shared virtual IP.
  • Layer 7 balancers can route by path; draining helps deploy without interrupting requests.
